claims.text: The initial alloy is equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW.
NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature strength, including near 1600 °C.
Single-phase NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
Experimental irradiation resistance has not been confirmed for NbMoTaW.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 5–10 at.% Ni, or a similar FCC-stabilizing element, to NbMoTaW.
Ni acts as an FCC-stabilizing addition in the proposed NbMoTaW composition range.
Adding 5–10 at.% Ni will produce nanometer-scale coherent FCC precipitates or discrete ductile FCC secondary phases within a BCC matrix.
The FCC secondary phase will provide additional slip systems and enhance dislocation mobility at room temperature.
Enhanced slip and dislocation mobility from the FCC phase will increase room-temperature ductility relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The FCC precipitates or secondary phases will act as irradiation-defect sinks and promote defect recombination.
The proposed defect-sink mechanism will reduce defect clustering, helium-bubble formation, blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation.
The residual BCC matrix will preserve high-temperature mechanical stability after the Ni addition.
The modified alloy will have higher room-temperature uniform elongation than untreated NbMoTaW.
The modified alloy will have lower irradiation-induced defect density and less blister formation than untreated NbMoTaW.
The modified alloy will retain strength and phase stability similar to untreated NbMoTaW up to approximately 1600 °C.
Helium exposure and high-energy neutron irradiation are representative hazards in fusion-reactor environments.
The proposed benefits are expected across approximately 300 K to 1600 °C under fusion-relevant irradiation.
The hypothesis is falsified by no statistically significant improvement in both ductility and irradiation tolerance, or by degradation of high-temperature performance relative to untreated NbMoTaW.

contradictions.description: The intervention is said to create a dual-phase BCC+FCC alloy while also preserving the phase stability of the single-phase base alloy. This is internally ambiguous unless 'phase stability' is restricted to retention of a stable BCC matrix rather than retention of the original single-phase state.
